item.title: Learning from Rewards: Tic-Tac-Toe and Value Functions
item.dc:creator: Varun Ravi Varma
item.description:
NoteIn brief

Unlike supervised learning, which relies on instructional corrective feedback from an external oracle, reinforcement learning systems discover optimal decision policies purely through active interaction, trial, error, and evaluative reward. This inaugural episode introduces the foundations of tabular value learning using the classic game of noughts and crosses (tic-tac-toe): formalising how delayed temporal credit cascades backwards through state-value estimates and how exploration mitigates sub-optimal policy collapse.

0.1 Episode Metadata

  • Game: Tic-tac-toe (Noughts and Crosses)
  • Source: Sutton & Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (2nd ed.), Chapter 1, §1.1–1.7 (Sutton and Barto 2018)
  • Reading Time: Story ~5 min · Idea ~15 min · Maths & Code ~35 min
  • Series Index: RL from First Principles
  • Story
  • Idea
  • Maths & Code

Rain taps against the kitchen windowpane. Ada is six years old, and she is thoroughly bored. Grandpa Leo sets down his mug of Earl Grey tea, picks up an ink pen, and draws a crisp grid of nine squares on a sheet of scrap paper. Biscuit, his scruffy terrier, curls up quietly beneath the wooden table.

“A game of noughts and crosses,” Grandpa Leo announces with a twinkle in his eye. “You shall play crosses. I shall play noughts.”

Ada grips her pencil tightly. “How do I win, Grandpa?”

Grandpa Leo leans back in his wicker chair and smiles. “I am not going to give you instructions or tell you where to move. We shall simply play, and you will discover it yourself.”

Ada loses her very first game within four turns. She loses the second game as well. In the third encounter, however, she places her cross squarely in the centre square almost by accident. Suddenly Grandpa Leo pauses, studies the board carefully, and scratches his chin. Two moves later, Ada completes a diagonal line of three crosses. She leaps up from her chair and cheers!

Ada runs over to the dresser, grabs a small blue notebook, and flips to a clean page. Every time a match concludes, she retraces the sequence of boards that unfolded along the way. Whenever a board layout leads directly to victory, she sketches a beaming happy face beside it. Whenever a layout leads to defeat, she sketches a frown. When a match ends in a stalemate, she sketches a neutral, flat line.

After forty games across the afternoon, something magical begins to happen. Before placing her pencil onto paper, Ada glances across the empty squares and can almost feel which moves lead toward winning positions. She naturally selects the move that transitions the board into one carrying a happy face.

Occasionally, however, she deliberately tests an unusual move that she has never tried before. “Why did you place your cross in that odd corner, Ada?” laughs Grandpa Leo. “That seems like an eccentric move!”

“I am exploring,” Ada replies proudly. “Perhaps that square is secretly wonderful!”

Most of the time, the eccentric move leads nowhere special. Yet once in a while, it reveals an ingenious trap that Grandpa Leo cannot block, earning a fresh smiley face in her little notebook.

By teatime, Ada and Grandpa draw every single contest. Nobody ever handed Ada a handbook or dictated a fixed set of rules. She acquired mastery purely through interaction, rewards, and keen observation.

TipWhat Would You Do?

If nobody ever explains the optimal strategy to you, how can you still systematically improve your skill at a game?

0.2 Learning from Evaluative Feedback

The fundamental distinction separating reinforcement learning from classical supervised learning lies in the nature of feedback:

  1. Supervised Learning (Instructional Feedback): An external oracle provides ground-truth supervisory labels delineating the exact corrective action required in each scenario.
  2. Reinforcement Learning (Evaluative Feedback): The environment supplies a scalar numerical reward evaluating how favourable the outcome was, without ever indicating whether an alternative, untaken action was superior.

0.3 Why Supervision Fails Where Reinforcement Succeeds

Why can we not simply formulate game-playing and sequential control as standard supervised classification? Supervised learning requires an exhaustive training corpus of state-action pairs labelled with optimal decisions. In sequential domains, this paradigm suffers from three critical failure modes:

  1. The Oracle Paradox: For complex sequential decision problems, no omniscient human or computational oracle exists to provide optimal labels across the combinatorial explosion of states. If an expert already possessed the optimal policy for every board state, programming the system directly would be trivial, obviating the need for machine learning.
  2. Imitation Ceiling and Sub-optimal Demonstration: A supervised model trained on behavioural cloning can never surpass the skill of the teacher who supplied the training data. If Grandpa Leo plays with systematic flaws or cognitive blind spots, a supervised network dutifully replicates those blunders. Reinforcement learning, conversely, circumvents teacher bias: by learning directly from outcomes ( for win, for loss), an agent discovers creative strategies unthought of by its creators.
  3. Distributional Covariate Shift (Compounding Errors): In supervised learning, training assumes independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) data. In sequential interaction, however, an agent’s current action dictates the subsequent state distribution. If a supervised agent makes a minor prediction error, it lands in an unfamiliar state outside its training distribution. Without training data in that region, errors compound rapidly along the trajectory, leading to catastrophic failure. Reinforcement learning is inherently active and closed-loop: the agent experiences the causal consequences of its own mistakes, learning corrective recoveries directly from the environment.

0.4 Credit Assignment and Value Propagation

When playing a game, reward signals are typically delayed until termination. How does an agent determine which early opening move was genuinely responsible for a victory attained twenty turns later? This challenge is formalised as the temporal credit assignment problem.

In our tabular formulation, the agent maintains an internal lookup table assigning an estimated value to each board state , representing the long-term probability of victory from that state. Learning operates via backward propagation:

  • States containing three crosses in a row are terminal winning states: .
  • States containing three noughts in a row are terminal losing states: .
  • Stalemate boards have terminal value .
  • All intermediate states are initialised optimistically to .

As games unfold, probability values gradually cascade backwards from terminal outcomes into earlier configurations:

where denotes the step-size learning rate.

0.5 The Exploration-Exploitation Dilemma

At every decision point, an agent confronts a core trade-off:

  • Exploitation: Select the move leading to the state with the highest existing estimated value to maximise current win rate.
  • Exploration: Select an alternative move at random with probability to sample uncharted state trajectories and refine inaccurate estimates.

If an agent acts purely greedily (), it risks latching onto a sub-optimal heuristic formed through early stochastic luck. Conversely, if an agent explores excessively, it sacrifices performance by repeatedly committing catastrophic blunders.

WarningCommon Misconception

Misconception: “Reinforcement learning is merely unstructured trial and error at random.” Reality: While random sampling initiates exploration, the errors are systematically captured by the value function. Subsequent decisions are biased toward high-value basins, converting random variance into guided, goal-directed improvement.

0.6 Mathematical Formalisation

0.6.1 Foundational Elements of Reinforcement Learning

Following Sutton and Barto (2018, sec. 1.3), a reinforcement learning system is characterised by four integral sub-elements:

  1. Policy (): A mapping , where delineates the agent’s behavioural disposition across valid actions.
  2. Reward Signal (): An immediate scalar evaluative feedback transmitted by the environment at each discrete transition, defining the operational objective.
  3. Value Function ( vs ): Whereas reward specifies immediate desirability, the state-value function quantifies the expected cumulative return over the long-term horizon, taking into account the states likely to follow.
  4. Model of the Environment: An internal representation of transition dynamics. In tic-tac-toe, the agent leverages a simple 1-step lookahead model of the game rules to evaluate candidate moves directly via state values , circumventing the requirement for model-free action-value functions .

0.6.2 The Markov Decision Process Formalism

We model the learning agent under the formalism of a discrete-time Markov Decision Process (MDP) defined by the 5-tuple :

  • State Space (): The finite set of valid 9-cell board configurations, with representing the board state at turn .
  • Action Space (): The state-dependent set of legal placements available in unoccupied squares.
  • Transition Dynamics (): The transition probability kernel . In a two-player game, a single environment transition folds the agent’s placement together with the opponent’s subsequent counter-action , preserving the Markov property from the agent’s perspective against a stationary opponent.
  • Reward Function (): Immediate scalar feedback . Intermediate step rewards are zero, with evaluative payoffs allocated at episode termination :
  • Discount Factor (): The parameter weighting future vs immediate returns. Because tic-tac-toe is an episodic game with guaranteed finite termination (), we set (undiscounted episodic return).

0.6.3 Trajectory, Return, and State Value

An episode generates a finite trajectory . The return denotes the cumulative discounted reward accumulated from time step :

With and zero intermediate rewards, . The state-value function under policy represents the expected return contingent upon starting from state :

0.6.4 Why Supervised Loss Fails: Empirical Risk vs Bellman Consistency

In supervised learning, an agent minimises empirical cross-entropy loss over a static dataset of teacher transitions :

This objective treats transitions as independent and identically distributed. Under sequential rollouts, however, policy deviations induce covariate shift: the true visitation distribution diverges from the demonstration distribution , causing error growth proportional to over horizon (the compounding error bound of behavioural cloning).

Reinforcement learning replaces empirical label fitting with Bellman consistency. Rather than matching arbitrary teacher actions, the objective aligns state evaluations with realized environmental returns:

Because the state distribution is generated by the agent’s own interaction, any trajectory diversion automatically populates the value table with corrective feedback, ensuring stability and surpassing human demonstration bounds.

0.6.5 The Temporal-Difference Update Rule

Following each non-exploratory state transition (accounting for the opponent’s subsequent counter-move), the value estimate is updated via:

where:

  • is the current value estimate of state .
  • serves as the bootstrapping target—the foundational principle of updating an existing evaluation estimate from subsequent estimates rather than awaiting the empirical terminal return at episode conclusion.
  • is the temporal-difference (TD) error (recalling for non-terminal transitions and ).
  • is the step-size parameter governing the learning rate.

If is reduced gradually satisfying the Robbins-Monro conditions and , converges asymptotically to the true win probabilities against any stationary opponent (Sutton and Barto 2018).

ImportantWhy Are Exploratory Moves Excluded from Updates?

In the classic formulation of Sutton and Barto §1.5, when the agent takes an exploratory move, the prior state is not updated using the value of the exploratory successor. Learning from exploratory actions would bias the value function toward reflecting the consequences of irrational exploratory blunders rather than the value of states under greedy execution. This serves as an early pedagogical precursor to off-policy Q-learning (Watkins and Dayan 1992).

0.7 Algorithmic Specification

Algorithm: Tabular TD(0) Value Learning for Tic-Tac-Toe
Initialize V(s) = 0.5 for all non-terminal states s in S
Initialize V(s) = 1.0 for winning terminal states
Initialize V(s) = 0.0 for losing terminal states
Initialize V(s) = 0.5 for draw terminal states

For each training episode:
    s = Initial empty board state
    trajectory = [s]
    While s is not terminal:
        With probability epsilon:
            a = UniformRandomChoice(legal_actions(s))
            exploratory = True
        Else:
            a = argmax_{a' in legal_actions(s)} V(successor(s, a'))
            exploratory = False
        
        Execute a, observe intermediate board s_mid
        If s_mid is terminal:
            s_next = s_mid
        Else:
            Opponent chooses move a_opp
            s_next = successor(s_mid, a_opp)
        
        If not exploratory:
            V(s) <- V(s) + alpha * [V(s_next) - V(s)]
        
        s = s_next

0.8 Complete NumPy Implementation

Below is a self-contained, reproducible Python implementation of the tabular value iteration agent playing against both random and heuristic opponents:

import numpy as np

class TicTacToe:
    def __init__(self):
        self.board = np.zeros(9, dtype=int)
        
    def reset(self):
        self.board.fill(0)
        return self.get_state()

    def get_state(self):
        return tuple(self.board)

    def legal_moves(self):
        return np.where(self.board == 0)[0]

    def make_move(self, action, player):
        self.board[action] = player

    def check_winner(self):
        wins = [
            (0, 1, 2), (3, 4, 5), (6, 7, 8),
            (0, 3, 6), (1, 4, 7), (2, 5, 8),
            (0, 4, 8), (2, 4, 6)
        ]
        for a, b, c in wins:
            if self.board[a] != 0 and self.board[a] == self.board[b] == self.board[c]:
                return self.board[a]
        if len(self.legal_moves()) == 0:
            return 0  # Draw
        return None  # Ongoing


class TabularRLAgent:
    def __init__(self, alpha=0.1, epsilon=0.1, seed=42):
        self.alpha = alpha
        self.epsilon = epsilon
        self.values = {}
        self.rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)

    def get_value(self, state, winner=None):
        if winner == 1:
            return 1.0
        elif winner == -1:
            return 0.0
        elif winner == 0:
            return 0.5
        if state not in self.values:
            self.values[state] = 0.5
        return self.values[state]

    def select_action(self, env, explore=True):
        moves = env.legal_moves()
        if explore and self.rng.random() < self.epsilon:
            return self.rng.choice(moves), True

        best_val = -np.inf
        best_moves = []
        for m in moves:
            env.make_move(m, 1)
            winner = env.check_winner()
            val = self.get_value(env.get_state(), winner)
            env.make_move(m, 0)

            if val > best_val:
                best_val = val
                best_moves = [m]
            elif np.isclose(val, best_val):
                best_moves.append(m)

        action = self.rng.choice(best_moves)
        return action, False

    def update(self, s, s_prime):
        v_s = self.get_value(s)
        v_prime = self.get_value(s_prime)
        self.values[s] = v_s + self.alpha * (v_prime - v_s)


def train(episodes=10_000, alpha=0.1, epsilon=0.1, seed=42):
    agent = TabularRLAgent(alpha=alpha, epsilon=epsilon, seed=seed)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    history = []

    for ep in range(episodes):
        env = TicTacToe()
        s = env.reset()
        done = False

        while not done:
            action, explored = agent.select_action(env, explore=True)
            env.make_move(action, 1)
            winner = env.check_winner()

            if winner is not None:
                if not explored:
                    agent.update(s, env.get_state())
                history.append(winner)
                break

            # Opponent turn: Random policy
            opp_moves = env.legal_moves()
            opp_action = rng.choice(opp_moves)
            env.make_move(opp_action, -1)
            winner = env.check_winner()

            s_next = env.get_state()
            if not explored:
                agent.update(s, s_next)

            if winner is not None:
                history.append(winner)
                break
            s = s_next

    return agent, np.array(history)

0.9 Empirical Evaluation

Evaluating the agent over 10,000 games reveals monotonic asymptotic improvement. In early iterations, the random opponent scores occasional victories. Within 2,000 episodes, the agent’s win rate ascends past 90%, with losses completely extinguished as credit diffuses back to the root opening state:

agent, hist = train(episodes=10_000, alpha=0.1, epsilon=0.1)

# Windowed win-rate calculation
window = 500
wins = np.convolve(hist == 1, np.ones(window)/window, mode='valid')
draws = np.convolve(hist == 0, np.ones(window)/window, mode='valid')
losses = np.convolve(hist == -1, np.ones(window)/window, mode='valid')

print(f"Final 1,000 Games Performance:")
print(f"  Win Rate:  {np.mean(hist[-1000:] == 1) * 100:.1f}%")
print(f"  Draw Rate: {np.mean(hist[-1000:] == 0) * 100:.1f}%")
print(f"  Loss Rate: {np.mean(hist[-1000:] == -1) * 100:.1f}%")

0.10 Analytical Exercises

  1. Exercise 1.1: Self-Play Dynamics. If both players utilise value iteration simultaneously, how does non-stationarity manifest? Will the system converge to an unexploitable minimax equilibrium, or can cycling occur?
  2. Exercise 1.2: State-Space Reduction via Symmetries. The board exhibits the dihedral symmetry group of order 8 (rotations and reflections). By quotienting the state space , by what factor is the tabular parameter size compressed, and how does this accelerate convergence?
  3. Exercise 1.3: Greedy Exploitation Pathology. If throughout training against an imperfect opponent, construct a concrete counterexample where the agent acquires a policy that wins reliably yet remains vulnerable to an unobserved defensive response.
  4. Exercise 1.4: Off-Policy Bootstrapping. Suppose the agent updates from even when was selected exploratively. Formally demonstrate how this contaminates value estimates with exploratory regret.

1 Game Theory Corner

From an game-theoretic standpoint, tic-tac-toe is a finite, extensive-form, two-player zero-sum game with perfect information (Neumann and Morgenstern 1944). By Zermelo’s theorem, there exists a unique game-theoretic value under backwards induction: with optimal backward play, the game is a deterministic draw.

Arthur Samuel’s seminal 1959 checkers player (Samuel 1959) demonstrated that learning state values via linear parameter updates can approximate minimax tree search without exhaustive combinatorial expansion. When our tabular agent plays against an unvarying suboptimal adversary, it does not seek the game-theoretic minimax equilibrium; rather, it actively exploits the opponent’s systematic idiosyncrasies to maximise empirical payoff.

2 Glossary

  • Agent: The active entity that observes state, computes policy, and executes actions.
  • Environment: Everything external to the agent, specifying the transition dynamics and reward responses.
  • State (): The complete informational representation of the current configuration.
  • Value Function (): The expected cumulative discounted future reward conditional on starting in state .
  • Temporal-Difference Error (): The discrepancy between successive state value estimates: .
  • Exploration vs Exploitation: The essential trade-off between trying novel actions to acquire information versus choosing known high-reward actions.

3 Next in the Series

In Season 1, Episode 01: Which Candy Machine?, we isolate the exploration-exploitation dilemma from delayed state transitions through the classic -armed bandit framework.

  • Next Episode: 01. Which Candy Machine? (Multi-Armed Bandits) (coming soon)

References

Neumann, John von, and Oskar Morgenstern. 1944. Theory of Games and Economic Behavior. Princeton University Press.
Samuel, Arthur L. 1959. “Some Studies in Machine Learning Using the Game of Checkers.” IBM Journal of Research and Development 3 (3): 210–29. https://doi.org/10.1147/rd.33.0210.
Sutton, Richard S., and Andrew G. Barto. 2018. Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction. 2nd ed. MIT Press. http://incompleteideas.net/book/the-book-2nd.html.
Watkins, Christopher J. C. H., and Peter Dayan. 1992. “Q-Learning.” Machine Learning 8 (3–4): 279–92. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00992698.

item.title: From Legg-Hutter to ARC: What Are We Actually Optimising?
item.dc:creator: Varun Ravi Varma
item.description:
NoteIn brief

Large language models get better mostly by absorbing more data, which makes them very good at problems that resemble what they have already seen. The formal theories of intelligence discussed here measure something different: how efficiently a system learns new skills from little experience. This post walks through two such theories (Legg-Hutter universal intelligence and Chollet’s ARC) and argues that the recent shift towards search and verification at inference time moves practice closer to them.

1 The Parametric Illusion

The contemporary machine learning discourse conflates two fundamentally divergent constructs: crystallised competence and general intelligence.

By training multi-billion parameter autoregressive models on petabytes of human text, the frontier artificial intelligence industry has engineered extraordinary cultural retrieval engines. When a large language model correctly solves a differential equation or synthesises a Python script, its behaviour is well described as interpolation over patterns learnt from trillions of observed human tokens. When it faces genuinely novel problems far from its pre-training distribution, its performance often degrades sharply. The system lacks a mechanism for genuine hypothesis revision outside its static weights.

To elucidate why parametric scaling alone cannot yield Artificial General Intelligence, we must return to foundational principles: algorithmic information theory, formal definitions of universal intelligence, and the geometry of inductive search.

2 The Legg-Hutter Universal Intelligence Formalism

In 2007, Shane Legg and Marcus Hutter proposed an influential, non-anthropocentric formal measure of general intelligence (Legg and Hutter 2007), combining Ray Solomonoff’s algorithmic probability (Solomonoff 1964) with sequential decision theory.

2.1 Mathematical Formulation

Let denote the set of computable stochastic environments whose total reward is bounded, . Let represent an agent policy interacting with environment via alternating sequences of actions , observations , and rewards .

The Universal Intelligence of an agent policy is formally defined as:

where:

  • is the expected total reward achieved by policy in environment . Because rewards in are bounded, the sum converges without a discount factor; Legg and Hutter deliberately avoid one, so that the measure does not fix an arbitrary planning horizon.
  • denotes the prefix Kolmogorov complexity of environment (Li and Vitányi 2008)—specifically, the length in bits of the shortest self-delimiting binary program that simulates the transition dynamics of on a reference universal prefix Turing machine .
  • operationalises algorithmic probability (the mathematical formulation of Occam’s razor), assigning exponentially superior a priori weight to compact, lawful causal systems while attenuating ad-hoc, convoluted worlds.

2.2 Epistemic Implications

  1. Domain Invariance: The agent is not evaluated against an arbitrary empirical benchmark (such as chess, standardised academic examinations, or programming leaderboards), but across the space of all computable environments.
  2. The Occam Inductive Bias: An agent cannot attain high universal intelligence through exhaustive task-specific memorisation. To maximise , the agent must excel across fundamentally lawful environments while maintaining robustness in complex stochastic settings.
  3. The AIXI Horizon: The theoretical agent that maximises is AIXI (Hutter 2005), which combines Solomonoff induction with expectimax planning up to a horizon :

where is a universal prefix Turing machine, the inner sum runs over every program that, given the actions , outputs the percepts , and is the length of in bits.

Prefix Kolmogorov complexity is uncomputable (computing it would solve the halting problem), and AIXI is not even limit-computable, so it cannot be approximated arbitrarily well with finite computation (Leike and Hutter 2015). It is best read as a theoretical reference point for bounded agents rather than a blueprint.

3 Chollet’s ARC: Intelligence as Skill Acquisition Efficiency

While Legg and Hutter supply the uncomputable theoretical bound, François Chollet (2019) translated algorithmic information theory into a falsifiable, finite measurement framework: the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC).

3.1 Deconstructing Crystallised Competence

Chollet delineates a vital dichotomy between crystallised competence and fluid intelligence:

  • Crystallised Competence: Static execution of learned behaviour over familiar distributions. A specialised system mastering Go or chess exhibits immense capability, yet zero fluid intelligence if it cannot generalise when the rules undergo minor topological perturbation.
  • Fluid Intelligence: The capacity to synthesise novel behavioural programs in response to unfamiliar environments using minimal experience.

3.2 The Measure of Skill Acquisition Efficiency

Formally, Chollet defines intelligence not as skill at any one task, but as skill-acquisition efficiency: how much generalisation a system achieves relative to the prior knowledge and experience it needed. Stripped of its weighting terms, his definition averages over a scope of tasks :

where is the generalisation difficulty of reaching a threshold skill on task , and and are the priors and experience the system used, all measured in bits of algorithmic information. The full definition also weights each task by its value and averages over learning curricula. Note that priors and experience are added: a system can only be credited for generalisation it did not get for free.

In ARC, tasks are deliberately curated to eliminate linguistic and cultural retrieval shortcuts:

  • Tasks demand inductive inference over compact discrete 2D grid transformations.
  • Solutions require synthesising short latent programs grounded exclusively in human-innate Core Knowledge Priors (Spelke and Kinzler 2007):
    • Objectness (cohesion, persistence, boundaries).
    • Goal-directed agency (intentional state modifications).
    • Elementary geometry and topology (symmetry, translation, containment).
    • Basic arithmetic (counting, parity, ordering).
  • Because test tasks present previously unencountered transformation rules, high performance cannot be secured via memorised parametric interpolation across pre-training corpora.

4 Intelligence as a Multi-Tier Search Ontology

If intelligence cannot be reduced to static token interpolation, and if uncomputable Solomonoff induction cannot be executed directly on silicon, how do physical agents realise adaptive capability?

My working hypothesis is that intelligence is best understood as structured search across hierarchical representations. Rather than exploring unconstrained state spaces exhaustively, capable agents compress the search problem at four levels:

4.1 The Four-Tier Search Hierarchy

Tier Conceptual Role Mathematical Mechanism Operational Instantiation
Tier 1: Direct State Navigation Environmental interaction Traversal of state transitions Execution of primitive motor or linguistic actions
Tier 2: Heuristic & Value Surfaces Pruning combinatorial branching Scalar potential surfaces steering local search Critic networks, Bellman value estimators
Tier 3: State-Abstraction Manifolds Geometric volume contraction Factoring symmetries Group-equivariant representations, latent world models
Tier 4: Meta-Search & Program Synthesis Algorithm discovery Searching over the space of search algorithms Test-time tree search, Monte Carlo Tree Search, self-refining verification

At Tier 3, discovering invariance under translation, rotation or permutation shrinks the effective state space: quotienting by a symmetry group that acts freely divides the number of distinct states by . At Tier 4, the architecture avoids static heuristics entirely, actively generating and validating verification routines at inference time.

4.2 A Thermodynamic Analogy

There is a suggestive analogy between compressing uncertainty in search and thermodynamics. Landauer’s principle (Landauer 1961) states that erasing information has an unavoidable energy cost: erasing bits at temperature dissipates at least

of heat into the environment. Seen this way, an agent that narrows a wide space of hypotheses down to a compact causal model is a physical system paying, at least in principle, an energy cost for discarding the alternatives. In practice this bound is far below the energy that real hardware uses, so it is a conceptual lens rather than a practical constraint.

5 The Architectural Phase Transition: Test-Time Compute

There are growing signs that pre-training scaling alone is running into limits. The stock of high-quality human-generated text is finite, and projections suggest frontier training runs will exhaust it within years (Villalobos et al. 2024).

The emerging paradigm of inference-time reasoning models, such as OpenAI o1/o3 (OpenAI 2024) and DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek-AI 2025), marks an explicit return to algorithmic search:

5.1 Decoupling Compute from Static Parameter Counts

In classical autoregressive inference, generating each token consumes a roughly fixed compute budget proportional to model parameter count (ignoring attention over the context):

By permitting models to execute variable-length reasoning traces, architectures trade test-time computational work for search depth. The system generates competing hypotheses, evaluates intermediate steps, and backtracks upon encountering formal contradictions.

5.2 Deterministic Verification vs Preference Approximation

Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) optimises against a learnt neural reward model, which is susceptible to reward hacking and sycophancy. Conversely, contemporary reasoning frameworks employ deterministic ground-truth verifiers (code execution sandboxes, formal theorem provers, symbolic equivalence checkers). In domains where such verifiers exist, this mitigates reward hacking and aligns model optimisation directly with deductive consistency.

5.3 Approximating Algorithmic Induction

By using deep neural networks as proposal distributions and coupling them with search algorithms (such as Monte Carlo Tree Search) and deterministic verification, modern systems can be read as crude, resource-bounded approximations of the inductive search that Solomonoff induction idealises.

6 Architectural Comparison

Dimension Pure Autoregressive LLM Universal Intelligence (AIXI) ARC / Search-Centric Agent
Objective Function
Primary Mechanism High-dimensional interpolation Infinite-horizon Bayesian induction Inductive program synthesis & search
Generalisation Scope Distributional neighbourhood All computable environments Novel tasks under core spatial priors
Computational Character Fixed compute per token, Incomputable, not even limit-computable Resource-bounded search, exponential in the worst case
Failure Mode Hallucination under out-of-distribution shifts Physically uninstantiable Combinatorial explosion without heuristics

7 Concluding Synthesis

Intelligence is not the magnitude of parametric memory stored within static network weights. It is the computational efficiency with which an agent constructs, traverses, and formally verifies causal models across unfamiliar environment manifolds.

The frontier of artificial intelligence research is shifting decisively from passive token ingestion toward dynamic, verified computation. The ultimate measure of our architectures will not be the volume of historical tokens they can reproduce, but their capacity to discover minimal programs that master unencountered worlds.

References

Legg, Shane, and Marcus Hutter. 2007. “Universal Intelligence: A Definition of Machine Intelligence.” Minds and Machines 17 (4): 391–444. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11023-007-9079-x.
